'''Lance Barrett-Lennard''' is a Canadian biologist specializing in the behavioural ecology and population biology of [[killer whale]]s. A molecular geneticist, Barrett-Lennard uses [[DNA]] analysis to study the dispersal, mating habits, and group structure of killer whale sub-populations in the [[Pacific Northwest]]. He is best known for his research concerning the conservation of the [[Southern resident killer whales|Southern Resident killer whale]] sub-population. As of 2022, he is a Senior Scientist in the Cetacean Conservation Research Program at the Raincoast Conservation Foundation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team members and staff |url=https://www.raincoast.org/team/ |access-date=2022-05-06 |website=Raincoast Conservation Foundation |language=en}}</ref>

== Education ==
Lance Barrett-Lennard attained a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[biology]] from the [[University of Guelph]] in Ontario (1976-1980), and went on to complete a Master of Science in biology at the [[University of British Columbia]] (1992). Barrett-Lennard also gained his doctorate at the University of British Columbia where he studied the role of genetics in the mating systems and population subdivisions of killer whales.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.zoology.ubc.ca/~barrett/|title=Dr. Lance Barrett-Lennard|website=www.zoology.ubc.ca|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref>

== Career ==
Following the completion of his Ph.D., Barrett-Lennard took a research scientist position with [[Fisheries and Oceans Canada]] (formerly DFO) at the [[Pacific Biological Station]] in [[Nanaimo]], British Columbia where he continued studying the role of genetics in the population structure of killer whale sub-populations. In 2001, he accepted a position as Director of the [[Marine mammal|Marine Mammal]] Research Program at the [[Vancouver Aquarium]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://killerwhale.vanaqua.org/page.aspx?pid=1359|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130814222036/http://killerwhale.vanaqua.org/page.aspx?pid=1359|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 14, 2013|title=Vancouver Aquarium|website=killerwhale.vanaqua.org|access-date=2019-11-01}}</ref>
[[File:Vancouver Aquarium - panoramio.jpg|thumb|The Vancouver Aquarium.]]

== Research ==
One of many research units at the Vancouver Aquarium, the Marine Mammal Research Program (MMRP) conducts research on Killer Whales, Humpback Whales, Harbour Porpoises, Beluga Whales, Sea Otters, and a host of other marine mammals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://research.ocean.org/program/marine-mammals|title=Ocean Wise Research|website=research.ocean.org|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref> A major branch of the MMRP is The B.C. Cetacean Sightings Network, a whale sightings report system that relies heavily on [[Citizen science]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wildwhales.org/|website=wildwhales.org|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref> The B.C. Cetacean Sightings Network facilitates the reporting of whale sightings through the WhaleReport mobile app. Details on whale locations are then used by the WhaleReport Alert System to notify nearby vessels of cetaceans in their vicinity and to encourage them to take precautionary or evasive action.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wildwhales.org/wras/|title=The WhaleReport Alert System {{!}} WildWhales|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref> Data from the B.C. Cetacean Sightings Network is also used to encourage the practice of land-based whale watching. In 2015, the B.C. Cetacean Sightings Network partnered with the Whale Trail, a Seattle-based organization dedicated on identifying potential land-based whale watching sites in the Pacific Northwest. Land-based whale watching is viewed as a zero-impact alternative to traditional boat-based whale watching. As of recent{{When|date=January 2020}}, the WhaleTrail B.C. has identified 39 such sites.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wildwhales.org/the-whale-trail-bc/|title=The Whale Trail BC {{!}} WildWhales|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref> In addition, sightings data is available to academic researchers, industry, and [[NGO]]s to aid conservation-based research projects. Discoveries involving sightings data include a newly discovered hot spot of [[Pacific white-sided dolphin]] in the [[Howe Sound]] area in 2010, and the discovery of a feeding ground utilized by [[Gray whale]]s in [[Baynes Sound]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wildwhales.org/sightings/how-sightings-are-used/|title=How Sightings Are Used {{!}} WildWhales|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref> [[File:Killer Whale chasing Chinook.jpg|thumb|Drone-captured photo of Southern Resident Killer Whale chasing a Chinook Salmon. (2017)]]Barrett-Lennard has made significant research contributions relating to the conservation of killer whales. Through DNA analysis, Barrett-Lennard and his colleagues have shown that the killer whale population in the northeastern Pacific ocean is divided into at least nine [[Sympatric speciation|sympatric]] sub-populations.<ref>{{Cite thesis|url=https://open.library.ubc.ca/cIRcle/collections/ubctheses/831/items/1.0099652|title=Population structure and mating patterns of Killer Whales (Orcinus orca) as revealed by DNA analysis|first=Lance Godfrey|last=Barrett-Lennard|date=October 31, 2000|publisher=University of British Columbia |doi=10.14288/1.0099652 |via=open.library.ubc.ca}}</ref> His research focuses on evidence of sympatric speciation in killer whale subpopulations inhabiting the northeastern Pacific. His work has shown that killer whale sub-populations vary significantly in their diet,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Foraging Strategies of Sympatric Killer Whale (orcinus Orca) Populations in Prince William Sound, Alaska|first1=Eva|last1=Saulitis|author1-link=Eva Saulitis |first2=Craig|last2=Matkin|first3=Lance|last3=Barrett-Lennard|first4=Kathy|last4=Heise|first5=Graeme|last5=Ellis|date=October 31, 2000|journal=Marine Mammal Science|volume=16|issue=1|pages=94–109|doi=10.1111/j.1748-7692.2000.tb00906.x|bibcode=2000MMamS..16...94S }}</ref> behaviour,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The mixed blessing of echolocation: differences in sonar use by fish-eating and mammal-eating killer whales|first1=LANCE G.|last1=Barrett-lennard|first2=JOHN K. B.|last2=Ford|first3=KATHY A.|last3=Heise|date=March 1, 1996|journal=Animal Behaviour|volume=51|issue=3|pages=553–565|doi=10.1006/anbe.1996.0059|s2cid=11867224}}</ref> and feeding grounds.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Use of chemical tracers in assessing the diet and foraging regions of eastern North Pacific killer whales|first1=Margaret M.|last1=Krahn|first2=David P.|last2=Herman|first3=Craig O.|last3=Matkin|first4=John W.|last4=Durban|first5=Lance|last5=Barrett-Lennard|first6=Douglas G.|last6=Burrows|first7=Marilyn E.|last7=Dahlheim|first8=Nancy|last8=Black|first9=Richard G.|last9=LeDuc|first10=Paul R.|last10=Wade|date=March 1, 2007|journal=Marine Environmental Research|volume=63|issue=2|pages=91–114|doi=10.1016/j.marenvres.2006.07.002|pmid=16934324|bibcode=2007MarER..63...91K |s2cid=2610041 |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1169&context=usdeptcommercepub}}</ref> His work has unveiled wide variability in the diet of killer whale sub-populations. Barrett-Lennard's most cited study showed that the [[Southern resident killer whale]] is primarily [[Piscivore|piscivorous]], and 96% of its diet is [[Salmonidae|salmonids]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Dietary specialization in two sympatric populations of killer whales (Orcinus orca) in coastal British Columbia and adjacent waters|first1=John KB|last1=Ford|first2=Graeme M|last2=Ellis|first3=Lance G|last3=Barrett-Lennard|first4=Alexandra B|last4=Morton|first5=Rod S|last5=Palm|first6=Kenneth C|last6=Balcomb III|date=August 1, 1998|journal=Canadian Journal of Zoology|volume=76|issue=8|pages=1456–1471|doi=10.1139/z98-089|bibcode=1998CaJZ...76.1456F }}</ref> The same study also discovered a distinct preference for mammalian prey by the Southern Transient Killer Whale sub-population.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ford|first1=John KB|last2=Ellis|first2=Graeme M|last3=Barrett-Lennard|first3=Lance G|last4=Morton|first4=Alexandra B|last5=Palm|first5=Rod S|last6=Balcomb III|first6=Kenneth C|date=1998-08-01|title=Dietary specialization in two sympatric populations of killer whales (Orcinus orca) in coastal British Columbia and adjacent waters|journal=Canadian Journal of Zoology|volume=76|issue=8|pages=1456–1471|doi=10.1139/z98-089|bibcode=1998CaJZ...76.1456F |issn=0008-4301}}</ref> He has also shown that offshore killer whales may prey on [[Pacific sleeper shark]], the first identified observation of the species being targeted as prey.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ford|first1=JKB|last2=Ellis|first2=GM|last3=Matkin|first3=CO|last4=Wetklo|first4=MH|last5=Barrett-Lennard|first5=LG|last6=Withler|first6=RE|date=2011-01-06|title=Shark predation and tooth wear in a population of northeastern Pacific killer whales|journal=Aquatic Biology|language=en|volume=11|issue=3|pages=213–224|doi=10.3354/ab00307|issn=1864-7782|doi-access=free|bibcode=2011AquaB..11..213F }}</ref> In 2008, Barrett-Lennard's research was used by the [[Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada|Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife]] to officially list the Southern Resident Killer Whale as an endangered species<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dfo-mpo.gc.ca/campaign-campagne/protectingwhales-protegerbaleines/srkw-eng.html|title=Protecting Southern Resident Killer Whales|first=Fisheries and Oceans Canada|last=Government of Canada|date=October 30, 2018|website=dfo-mpo.gc.ca}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wildlife-species.canada.ca/species-risk-registry/species/speciesDetails_e.cfm?sid=699|title=Species Profile (Killer Whale) - Species at Risk Public Registry|website=wildlife-species.canada.ca|access-date=2019-11-01}}</ref>
Barrett-Lennard's most recent work focuses on the use of drone-based aerial [[photogrammetry]] to remotely observe health and body condition of killer whales.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://research.ocean.org/project/body-condition-of-killer-whales|title=Ocean Wise Research - Body Condition of Killer Whales|website=research.ocean.org|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref> His team has shown that images captured by drones can be used to estimate blubber fat reserves and subsequently body condition by analyzing features such as head shape and eyepatch proportions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fearnbach|first1=Holly|last2=Durban|first2=John W.|last3=Barrett-Lennard|first3=Lance G.|last4=Ellifrit|first4=David K.|last5=Balcomb|first5=Kenneth C.|title=Evaluating the power of photogrammetry for monitoring killer whale body condition|journal=Marine Mammal Science|year=2020|volume=36|issue=1 |language=en|pages=359–364|doi=10.1111/mms.12642|bibcode=2020MMamS..36..359F |issn=1748-7692|doi-access=free}}</ref> Barrett-Lennard has also used drones to remotely monitor the respiratory microbiome of killer whales by aerially capturing samples of exhaled breath or "blow" <ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Apprill|first1=Amy|last2=Miller|first2=Carolyn A.|last3=Moore|first3=Michael J.|last4=Durban|first4=John W.|last5=Fearnbach|first5=Holly|last6=Barrett-Lennard|first6=Lance G.|date=2017-10-31|title=Extensive Core Microbiome in Drone-Captured Whale Blow Supports a Framework for Health Monitoring|journal=mSystems|language=en|volume=2|issue=5|article-number=e00119-17 |doi=10.1128/mSystems.00119-17 |doi-access=free|issn=2379-5077|pmid=29034331|pmc=5634792}}</ref>
[[File:Aerial Killer Whales.jpg|thumb|Drone-captured photo of two Southern Resident Killer Whales. (2015)]]

== Outreach ==
Barrett-Lennard has been a featured speaker at the annual B.C Marine Mammal Symposium in Vancouver, British Columbia. Barrett-Lennard has also shared his research with [[CBC News]]<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.cbc.ca/news/technology/pacific-white-sided-dolphins-southern-resident-killer-whales-1.5021585| title = Killer whales eat dolphins. So why are these dolphins tempting fate? {{!}} CBC News}} </ref> and [[CTV News]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/sci-tech/article/two-endangered-bc-orcas-expected-to-starve-by-summer/|title=Two endangered B.C. orcas expected to starve by summer &#124; CTV News|website=www.ctvnews.ca|date=4 January 2019 }}</ref> He has also voiced his scientific opinion on the controversial [[Harbor seal]] cull<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://vancouversun.com/opinion/op-ed/peter-ross-and-lance-barrett-lennard-harbour-seals-are-easy-scapegoats-in-chinook-salmon-decline|title=Opinion: Harbour seals are easy scapegoats in Chinook salmon decline &#124; Vancouver Sun|work=vancouversun |date=July 31, 2018}}</ref> and the [[Trans Mountain Pipeline]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/trans-mountain-pipeline-work-destroyed-salmon-habitat-puts-orcas-at-risk-mike-pearson/|title=Pipeline Work Destroyed Salmon Habitat, Puts Orcas at Risk, Scientists Say|first=Mirjam|last=Guesgen|date=January 30, 2019}}</ref> Barrett-Lennard is arguably most well known for documenting the link between the decline of [[Chinook salmon]] in the [[Pacific Northwest]] and the endangered status of the southern resident killer whale through aerial images of starving individuals<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/2-more-killer-whales-will-likely-die-by-summer-experts-say-1.4965171|title='Grandmother' Killer Whale is at risk of starvation - CBC}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/2-more-killer-whales-will-likely-die-by-summer-experts-say-1.4965171|title=2 more killer whales will likely die by summer - CBC}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/sci-tech/article/two-endangered-bc-orcas-expected-to-starve-by-summer/|title=Two endangered B.C. orcas expected to starve by summer - CTV}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://vancouversun.com/news/local-news/researchers-worried-killer-whale-population-will-flatline-with-female-deaths|title=Researchers worried killer whale population will flatline with female deaths - Vancouver Sun}}</ref>
